title: An animal’s story
what: A lineage’s fossil finds told as a story on the globe: where its kinds were found as the continents moved, how warm it was where they lay, which kinds began and ended, and whether land joined the continents it reached.
how: The Paleobiology Database’s classification joins each genus (a kind) to its family, order and so on, and its finds are grouped into sites every 5 million years, where they lay then on the PALEOMAP reconstruction. Each site also carries the part of today’s world its finds are in, read from where they are today in boxes good to a continent, and the mean annual temperature there then, read from Scotese’s map of that age. A kind counts as known from its first finds to its last, or to today if the database marks it as living. The doors between continents are read from PALEOMAP’s elevation maps: places inside each of today’s lands are carried back on the PALEOMAP plate model by the GPlates Web Service, each cell above sea level goes to the land nearest over such cells, and two lands are joined where their cells touch; a shallow sea lies between where they touch only once cells up to about 130 m deep count too. Silhouettes are PhyloPic’s, kept only when they are of the kind itself or a species in it; pictures are the lead pictures of Wikipedia’s articles, shown from Wikimedia Commons with their authors and licences. The moments a story stops at are found by rule in these numbers, not written by hand.
others: These are finds, not ranges: a kind found on one continent lived wherever it lived, and far more has been dug in North America and Europe than elsewhere, so an absence may be a gap in the digging. The classification is a taxonomy, not a dated family tree, and it does not yet hold living species’ ranges or the splits DNA dates. The temperatures are one model’s, and the 65-million-year map is left out as an outlier. The doors are the maps’ own reading at one sea level for each 5 million years, smoothed to 0.2°, and can differ from the geological literature: South America and Antarctica, held to have been joined until about 35 to 50 million years ago, read as apart; Africa and Eurasia read as joined earlier than the usual date of about 20 million years ago. A door open is a way a lineage could have walked, not proof that it did. Wikipedia’s lead picture may show a fossil, an artist’s reconstruction or a living relative.
